wordsPreamble:
- English is essentially universal here and spoken very well. Anything you attempt in Swedish is pure courtesy, and it’s received as one.
- There is no everyday word for “please.” Politeness lives in tone, and in the thank-you word, which does a remarkable amount of work.
- Sk and sj before soft vowels make a sound English doesn’t have, somewhere between h and sh. Approximating it is completely fine.
- Å, Ä, and Ö are separate letters and they’re all over the map. Ö is roughly the vowel in “her.”

- Not the Spanish you hear in Madrid. Andalusians drop final s, soften consonants, and run words together — faster and flatter.
- The Madrid “th” mostly disappears here. Seville says *gracias* closer to *GRAH-see-ah* than *GRAH-thee-ahs*.
- Less English than Madrid or Barcelona. Seville is a working city rather than one performing for visitors.
- Say hello walking into any shop or bar and goodbye on the way out. It matters as much here as in Madrid, possibly more.

- Standard Italian works everywhere. Neapolitan is a separate language, spoken constantly around you, and not something you’ll follow.
- English is thinner here than in Rome or Florence, and Naples isn’t performing for visitors the way they do.
- Neapolitan clips the ends off words: *mozzarella* becomes *muzzarell*, *Napoli* becomes *Napule*. You’ll hear it everywhere.
- Double consonants are held twice as long, and it changes the word.

- The southern accent is real. Final e’s get pronounced where Paris drops them, and nasal vowels end on a hard “-ng” — *pain* comes out *peng*.
- Marseille is far less formal than Paris. The greeting ritual still matters walking into a shop, but the rest of the stiffness doesn’t.
- English is thinner than in Paris, especially away from the Vieux-Port.
- This is a Mediterranean port with a large North African population. You’ll hear Arabic and Comorian alongside French.

- Munich speaks standard German to visitors, with a Bavarian accent and a set of southern greetings. Reaching for the northern ones is understood, just marked.
- Use *Sie* with anyone you don’t know, and greet people when you walk into a shop or bakery. Bavarian manners run more formal than the beer halls suggest.
- English is widely spoken in the centre, by younger people and in hotels and museums, and thinner in old Wirtshäuser and among older locals.
- *ei* is “eye” and *ie* is “ee.” *St* and *sp* at the start of a word are “sht” and “shp,” and ß is simply a double s.

- Brussels is officially bilingual and everything written appears in French and Dutch. In practice the city runs in French, and that’s what’s below.
- English is very widely spoken — this is an EU capital and a large share of residents were born elsewhere.
- Belgian French is close to the Paris version, with two differences worth knowing: “septante” is seventy and “nonante” is ninety.
- The greeting ritual is softer than Paris. Greet people walking in and the rest of the stiffness doesn’t apply.

- Warsaw speaks standard Polish, with little regional accent, and more English than anywhere else in Poland, especially among people under forty.
- Use “pan” (sir) and “pani” (madam) with strangers and people behind counters. The informal form is for friends and people your age.
- Greet people in shops with “dzień dobry” and say “do widzenia” leaving. Skipping it reads as rude.
- *sz* is “sh,” *cz* is “ch,” *w* is “v,” *ł* is “w,” and *rz* sounds like the s in “pleasure.” Stress almost always falls on the second-to-last syllable.

- English, with an Ulster accent that runs fast and moves its vowels around. Irish and Ulster Scots turn up on some signs; neither is widely spoken day to day.
- Belfast is friendly and direct, and strangers will talk to you at bus stops. The humour is dry and teasing, and being slagged off by a new friend is a good sign.
- Words carry sides here. Place names, flags, football shirts and Derry versus Londonderry all signal something, so follow how the person you’re talking to says it.
- Prices are in pounds sterling. Northern Irish banks print their own notes, which look unfamiliar but spend the same.

- English, spoken with Scouse, the fast, sing-song Liverpool accent shaped by Irish and Welsh migrants and the port. It sounds nothing like Manchester, 30 miles away, and locals would rather you didn’t compare them.
- Liverpool talks. Strangers chat at bus stops and bars, and teasing is friendly. A quick reply goes down better than a polite one.
- The city is red or blue: Liverpool FC or Everton. Families split down the middle, and someone will ask which you support.
- Many shops won’t sell *The Sun* newspaper, over its false 1989 coverage of the Hillsborough disaster, a stadium crush in which 97 Liverpool fans died. It is not a subject for jokes.

- English, with a Glasgow accent and a set of Scots words that visitors from England find harder than Edinburgh’s. People will slow down if you ask.
- Glasgow is famously open. Strangers start conversations at bus stops and in pub queues, and a short answer reads as unfriendly rather than polite.
- The humour is dry, quick and often at someone’s expense, including yours. Giving some back is expected.
- Football runs deep. Celtic and Rangers are a divide with religious and political history, so don’t pick a side casually or wear either strip into a pub.

- Milan speaks standard Italian with a northern accent. The old Milanese dialect survives mostly among older people and in a handful of phrases everyone knows.
- An *s* between vowels is buzzed like a z here: *casa* sounds like “kaza.” Every letter is still pronounced, and double consonants are held longer.
- English is common in the centre, in business and fashion, and in hotels. Milan is Italy’s working city and moves quickly, so keep exchanges short and polite.
- Greet people entering a shop or bar, and again on the way out. Coffee is drunk standing at the counter, and fast.

- English is standard in the centre, where visitors far outnumber the fewer than 50,000 people who still live in the historic city.
- Among themselves, many locals speak Venetian, not Italian. You’ll hear it at bars and markets; nobody expects you to.
- Street signs are painted on white wall patches called *nizioleti*, in Venetian: *calle* for street, *rio* for canal, *fondamenta* for a canal-side walk.
- Addresses are a district and a number, such as *Castello 5000*, numbered across the whole district. Use a map, not the number.
- Greet people entering a shop or bar, and again on the way out.

- Nearly everyone in central Lisbon speaks good English. Your Portuguese is a courtesy, not a tool — two words go a long way and no one expects more.
- Say final *s* as “sh.” Lisboa is *lish-BOH-uh*. It’s the one change that makes you sound less like a tourist.
- Portuguese is shorter out loud than it looks on the page. Swallow the endings instead of pronouncing every letter.
- If you’ve picked up any Portuguese from Brazilian sources, it’ll land as noticeably from-somewhere-else here.

- English, with a dialect stronger than visitors expect, and stronger again the further out from the centre you go.
- Manchester is direct and warm at once, and far less reserved than London. Strangers will talk to you on buses.
- None of this is Cockney. Rhyming slang is a London thing and using it here will only confuse people.
- Football isn’t small talk. It’s a real dividing line, and someone will ask which side you’re on.

- English, with Scots woven through it — not an accent but a set of words that have no English equivalent.
- Gaelic appears on station signs and official buildings. It isn’t spoken here and isn’t related to Scots.
- Edinburgh is more reserved than Glasgow and will tell you so itself. The formality is real and isn’t coldness.
- In August the city roughly triples for the Festival. Prices, queues, and everyone’s patience change accordingly.

- English, with Irish printed on every sign underneath it. You’ll read Irish constantly and hear it almost never.
- The rhythm differs from British English. Sentences lift at the end, and questions get answered with a full sentence rather than yes or no.
- Nobody expects you to attempt Irish. Pronouncing it wrong is the norm among Dubliners too.
- Slagging — relentless mock insults between friends — is affection. Taking it personally is the only real mistake available.

- You share a language and will still be caught out. What follows are words that mean something different here, not words you can’t understand.
- Queue for everything, including at a bus stop where there’s no visible line. People are tracking the order in their heads.
- Stand on the right on escalators. Walking on the left is the entire system and blocking it is the one thing that gets a reaction.
- Nobody will correct you. The response to a mistake is a small silence, not a comment, so you may never find out.

- English is common in Sultanahmet, Beyoğlu, and anything tourist-facing, and drops off quickly beyond them.
- Turkish uses the Latin alphabet and is spelled exactly as it sounds. Once you know a few letters you can read any sign aloud.
- C is “j” as in jam, and Ç is “ch.” So *Caddesi* is *jahd-DEH-see* and *Beşiktaş* is *beh-SHEEK-tash*.
- The undotted ı is a swallowed “uh,” different from the dotted i. Both turn up constantly, including in capitals.

- English is heavy in the centre — Florence takes more visitors per resident than almost anywhere in Europe — and drops off sharply across the river.
- Tuscans soften a hard c between vowels into an h. *La casa* comes out closer to *la hasa*. It’s the local accent, not a mistake.
- Double consonants are held twice as long, and it changes the word.
- Greet people entering a shop or bar, and again on the way out.

- Catalan and Spanish are both official and both are everywhere. Signs and menus lean Catalan; conversation goes either way and nobody minds which you pick.
- Almost no visitor attempts Catalan, so the words below land considerably harder than their Spanish equivalents would.
- English is common in the centre and the Eixample, and thins in the outer neighbourhoods.
- X is “sh” in Catalan, so *Xavier* is *shah-vee-AY*. Unstressed vowels blur toward “uh,” and final consonants land hard.

- English is common with younger people and in the centre, and much less so elsewhere.
- If you have any Italian or Spanish you’ll recognise more here than anywhere else in this part of Europe.
- Ș is “sh” and Ț is “ts,” and both are everywhere. București is *boo-koo-RESHT*.
- Stress isn’t marked and isn’t regular, so the respellings below matter more than usual.

- English is common in the Old Town and Kazimierz, and thins fast beyond them.
- Stress lands on the second-to-last syllable of every word. That one habit does most of the work.
- Sz is “sh,” cz is “ch,” w is “v,” and ł is “w.” So Wisła is *VEE-swah*.
- Long consonant clusters are normal and less impossible than they look. Say them slowly and they come apart.

- English is widespread in the centre and drops off within a few tram stops.
- Czech is spelled as it sounds once you know the marks. The háček (ˇ) turns c into “ch,” s into “sh,” z into “zh.”
- Stress lands on the first syllable of every word, however long the word gets.
- Ř is a sound no other language has, somewhere between “rzh” and a rolled r. Nobody expects you to manage it.

- Serbian is written in two alphabets, Cyrillic and Latin, and both are official. The same street can be signed either way, sometimes both at once.
- English is common with younger people and in the centre, and much less so beyond it.
- Serbian is spelled exactly as it sounds — one letter, one sound, no exceptions. Once you know the letters you can read anything aloud.
- Č and Ć are both “ch,” Š is “sh,” Ž is “zh,” and J is “y.”

- English is widespread in central Athens and anywhere tourist-facing. A few streets out it thins quickly.
- You won’t be able to read anything, and that’s the real adjustment. Major routes are signed in Latin letters too; side streets aren’t.
- Some Greek letters look Latin and aren’t: Ρ is R, Η is I, Υ is roughly ee, Χ is a throaty H.
- Every word carries a stress mark telling you which syllable to hit. Getting the stress right matters more than getting the sounds right.

- English is universal and excellent. Icelandic is genuinely difficult and nobody expects a visitor to attempt it, which is exactly why trying lands well.
- Icelanders don’t use surnames the way you do. Phone books, staff lists, and name tags all run on first names.
- Þ is “th” as in thing; Ð is “th” as in this. Both turn up constantly on signs and place names.
- Ll is a “tl” sound. Long place names aren’t as impossible as they look, just long.

- English is universal here and excellent. Finns switch to it instantly and think nothing less of you.
- Every street sign is in two languages, Finnish first and Swedish second. The Finnish is what you’ll actually hear.
- Stress lands on the first syllable of every word, without exception.
- Doubled letters are held longer and change the word: *tuli* is fire, *tuuli* is wind, *tulli* is customs.

- English is universal and excellent. Norwegian is a courtesy here rather than a requirement.
- Norway has two written standards and a great many dialects, so nobody expects consistency. Say it roughly and you’ll be fine.
- There is no everyday word for “please.” Politeness lives in tone and in the thank-you word.
- Æ, Ø, and Å appear on every sign and map. Ø is roughly the vowel in “her”; Å is “oh.”

- English is close to universal and Danes speak it very well. Your Danish is a gesture, and it lands warmly precisely because so few visitors try.
- Danish is pronounced far less than it’s written. Endings vanish and consonants soften into vowels, so words are much shorter out loud.
- There is no everyday word for “please.” Politeness lives in tone and in the thank-you word, which Danes say constantly.
- Ø and Å are all over the map. Ø is roughly the vowel in “her”; Å is “oh.”

- Austrian German, not German German. Several everyday words are genuinely different, and reaching for the Berlin ones marks you as a visitor from the wrong direction.
- Formality reads as warmth here rather than distance. When in doubt, go more formal, not less.
- English is common in the centre and in coffeehouses, and thinner in the outer districts.
- *ei* is “eye” and *ie* is “ee.” *St* at the start of a word is “sht,” and ß is simply a double s.

- English is everywhere in central Berlin, more than in any other German city — plenty of café staff don’t speak German either.
- Greet people entering small shops and bakeries. Berlin is blunter than the rest of Germany but it still expects this.
- *ei* is “eye” and *ie* is “ee” — so *Bier* is beer and *Wein* is vine. Easy to swap, and it changes the word.
- *St* at the start of a word is “sht.” *Straße* is *SHTRAH-suh*, and ß is simply a double s.

- English is common around the tourist centre and thins out fast a few streets away.
- Every letter gets pronounced. Italian is forgiving — approximate it and you’ll be understood.
- Double consonants are held twice as long, and it changes the word: *pena* is a shame, *penna* is a pen.
- Greet people entering a shop or a bar, and again on the way out. It’s close to automatic here.

- Greet people before you say anything else — entering a shop, approaching a counter, boarding a bus. Skipping it is the single thing that reliably gets you treated badly, and it’s what visitors skip most.
- Less English than you’d expect for a city this size, and staff often won’t switch to it until you’ve greeted them properly.
- Final consonants mostly go silent. Paris is *pah-REE*, and the *s* on the end of *vous* and *plus* disappears.
- The French R is a soft scrape at the back of the throat, closer to gargling than to an English R. Nobody minds if you approximate it.

- Two languages are running at once. Everything **written** — menus, signs, tickets, bathroom doors — is standard German. Everything **spoken** is Swiss German. You don’t need to bridge them, only to know which one you’re looking at.
- Everyone understands standard German and most speak good English, so you can’t go wrong. But tourists almost never attempt the Swiss words, so the handful below land harder here than anywhere else.
- Greet people when you walk in: a shop, a lift, a small waiting room. Zurich does it reliably and notices when you don’t.
- Swiss German scrapes where German doesn’t: **ch** is a throat sound, in *Züri* and *Chuchi*. And it shrinks things — a *Sack* becomes a *Säckli*.

- English is close to universal here — better than most visitors expect. You will never actually need Dutch, which is exactly why the little you use registers as pure courtesy.
- Dutch people switch to English the second they hear an accent. It isn’t a rebuff, it’s efficiency. Say your word anyway.
- **G** is a scrape at the back of the throat, not an English hard G. It’s in *gracht*, *gezellig*, and *Van Gogh* — locals say that name nothing like you do.
- **IJ** is one sound, roughly “ay.” The Rijksmuseum is *RAYKS-mew-zay-um*, and the IJ is also the stretch of water behind Centraal.

- Nobody expects you to try. Hungarian has a reputation for being impossible, so even a mangled *köszönöm* gets a genuine reaction.
- Hit the first syllable of every word, hard. That habit does more for you than getting the individual sounds right.
- *S* is “sh.” Budapest is *BOO-dah-pesht*, the baths are *SAY-chen-yee*. Handy for reading signs.
- English is common under about 40 and rare above it.

- Say hello walking into a shop or a bar, and say goodbye on the way out. Skipping it reads as rude here in a way it wouldn’t in most of Europe.
- Less English than Lisbon or Amsterdam, especially a few streets off the center. Your handful of words will get real use.
- Vowels stay short and flat — ah, eh, ee, oh, oo. No English drifting. That alone gets you most of the way.
- *Z* and soft *C* are “th.” *Cerveza* is *thehr-VEH-thah*. It’s Madrid, not a lisp.
